text: After that night Adolph Myers came to Winesburg to live with his aunt, an old woman who raised chickens, and he stayed in her house until she died. <break time="0.8s" /> Although he was only forty, he looked sixty five, and he had taken the name Biddlebaum from a box of goods he had seen at a freight station. <break time="0.8s" /> He did not understand what had happened, but he felt that his hands must be to blame, and ever since then he had tried to hide them. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening Wing walked up and down his veranda until the sun had set and the road beyond the field was lost in grey shadows. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, still alone, he went into his house, cut slices of bread, and spread honey upon them for his simple supper. <break time="0.8s" /> When the rumble of the evening train that carried away the days harvest of berries had passed, the silence of the summer night returned, and he washed his dishes. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, kneeling by the table in the lamplight, he picked up the stray bread crumbs one by one and carried them to his mouth with amazing speed. <break time="0.8s" /> In that small circle of light under the table, he looked like a priest at prayer, and his quick, expressive fingers moved like those of a believer counting the beads of a rosary.
